label: Handmade / Sandstock Brick
volunteer_identification_guide: Moulded by hand in wet wooden moulds; distinctive irregular surfaces, fold creases along sides, thumb drag marks, hack marks from drying, no frog or shallow frog, slightly thinner (c. 60-65mm).

label: Machine-pressed / Wire-cut Brick
volunteer_identification_guide: Extruded through dies and cut with wire or dry-pressed in hydraulic steam presses; sharp crisp edges, uniform standard dimensions (c. 225x110x75mm), deep indent frog.

label: Stretcher Bond
volunteer_identification_guide: All bricks laid showing long side (stretcher) only; universally used in cavity walls and modern brick veneer; cannot form solid single-leaf structural wall without ties.

label: English Bond
volunteer_identification_guide: Alternating courses of all-headers (short ends) and all-stretchers (long sides); exceptionally strong bond common in civil engineering, warehouses, and early substantial buildings.

label: Flemish Bond
volunteer_identification_guide: Each course consists of alternating headers and stretchers; highly decorative, favoured for primary facades of Georgian and Victorian homesteads.

label: Colonial / Garden Wall Bond
volunteer_identification_guide: Three, four, or five courses of stretchers to every single course of headers; economical colonial method conserving expensive header brickwork.

label: Ashlar Masonry
volunteer_identification_guide: Finely dressed, squared stone blocks laid with hair-thin joints in level regular courses; high status craftsmanship.

label: Coursed Rubble
volunteer_identification_guide: Roughly squared rubble stones laid in identifiable horizontal courses of uniform or variable bed heights.

label: Random / Uncoursed Rubble
volunteer_identification_guide: Unshaped, irregular stones laid without horizontal continuous bed lines, gaps wedged with small spalls and mortar.

label: Soft Lime-Sand Mortar
volunteer_identification_guide: Creamy white or buff coloured, soft enough to scratch easily with a copper coin or fingernail; consists of slaked lime and coarse local sand.

label: Mud / Clay Mortar
volunteer_identification_guide: Brown, earthy mortar mixed with local loam, straw, or manure; common in vernacular stone outbuildings, chimneys, and pise cores.

label: Hard Grey Portland Cement Mortar
volunteer_identification_guide: Dark grey, very hard, cannot be scratched by thumbnail; imported from 1860s, locally manufactured from 1890s; post-1890 repair or late masonry.

label: Dressed Stone Quoins
volunteer_identification_guide: Larger squared dressed stones at external corners of rubble masonry or brickwork, often alternating in size (long-and-short work).

label: Contrasting Brick Quoins
volunteer_identification_guide: Face brick corner dressings contrasting with rubble stone walling or polychrome brick bodies.

label: Rendered / Rusticated Quoins
volunteer_identification_guide: Stucco plaster moulded and scored at building corners to imitate dressed stone ashlar blocks.

label: No Distinct Quoins
volunteer_identification_guide: Corners finished flush with the standard walling material without decorative or structural corner blocks.

label: Weatherboard - Beaded / Quirked Edge
volunteer_identification_guide: Horizontal overlapping weatherboards featuring a moulded bead along lower outer edge; diagnostic indicator of pre-1860 craftsmanship.

label: Weatherboard - Plain Splayed
volunteer_identification_guide: Standard wedge-shaped weatherboard with plain bevelled or square bottom edge; superseded beaded boards from 1860 onwards.

label: Rough-sawn Boarding / Clapboard
volunteer_identification_guide: Ungrooved flat sawn boards nailed horizontally or vertically with visible circular or pit saw marks.

label: Corrugated Iron - 5-inch (130mm) Early Pitch
volunteer_identification_guide: Heavy gauge corrugated galvanised sheet with broad 5-inch (130mm) crest-to-crest pitch; imported 1850-1860s, rare survivor of early gold era.

label: Corrugated Iron - 3-inch (80mm) Standard Pitch
volunteer_identification_guide: Standard 3-inch (c. 76-80mm) pitch corrugated iron; introduced in 1860s and universal cladding across rural Australia for over a century.

label: Ripple Iron (25mm Miniature Flutes)
volunteer_identification_guide: Fine corrugated iron with mini-pitch (c. 20-25mm); introduced c. 1890 for verandah ceilings, valances, internal dados, and meathouses.

label: Flattened Tin Plate (Kerosene / Petrol Tins)
volunteer_identification_guide: Square flattened sheet metal from recycled 4-gallon kerosene or motor spirit tins; soldered or nailed with diamond pattern, classic bush improvisation.

label: Fibro / Asbestos-Cement Sheet & Battens
volunteer_identification_guide: Flat grey rigid sheets (Wunderlich Durabestos / Hardies Fibrolite) with timber cover battens over joints; asbestos hazard; post-1903.

label: Limewash / Whitewash
volunteer_identification_guide: Thin breathable white or tinted slaked lime wash applied over slabs, masonry, pise, or brick; chalks off on hands.

label: Stucco / Cement Render (Scored)
volunteer_identification_guide: Smooth or ashlar-scored exterior mortar plaster coating brick or rubble stone to simulate fine masonry.

label: Roughcast / Pebbledash Render
volunteer_identification_guide: Coarse mortar plaster containing pebbles, gravel, or coarse aggregate thrown onto wall; characteristic of Edwardian / Arts and Crafts periods.
